chunks: Then he (peace be upon him) said:

Woe to your inhabited streets, and your decorated houses which have wings like the wings of vultures and trunks like the trunks of elephants; [they are] from those people whose killed are not mourned, and whose missing are not searched for.
I turn this world over on its face, value it only according to its (low) value, and look at it with an eye suitable to it.
ai.seo_question: What does Imam Ali mean by describing houses with wings of vultures and trunks of elephants?
ai.summary: Imam Ali (peace be upon him) critiques the architectural grandeur of Basra—specifically its multi-storied houses and elephant-trunk beams—as outward manifestations of spiritual arrogance and social indifference, where the death of the righteous goes unwept. This passage, often linked to the era of the Umayyads and later interpreted as foreshadowing the Mongol conquests, highlights his role as the 'conqueror of the world' who perceives its fleeting nature with divine clarity. The imagery underscores the Shia scholarly view that material excess often correlates with a loss of communal piety and vigilance.

en.sayed-ali-raza: Woe to you (the people of Baṣrah’s) inhabited streets and decorated houses which possess wings like the wings of vultures and trunks like the trunks of elephants; they are the people from among whom if one is killed he is not mourned and if one is lost he is not searched for.
I turn this world over on its face, value it only according to its (low) value, and look at it with an eye suitable to it.
